clue.text: Sweet smell attracts insect

parts.note: to hum is informal British for to give off a bad smell
a bug is any small insect

explanation.surface: A sugary scent draws in a passing insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attracts' only joins the two parts, as if the smell were pulling in the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A humbug is a hard striped British boiled confection, usually peppermint flavoured.

clue.text: It's rare, although Tom Jones begs to differ?

parts.note: surface reading: a plain statement that something seldom happens

parts.words: although Tom Jones begs to differ
parts.note: setter's reading: the Welsh singer's 1965 hit insists the opposite, It's Not ...

explanation.walkthrough: Tom Jones's signature song is 'It's Not Unusual', so he would disagree with calling it rare.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare is seldom seen or found, which is what an uncommon or unusual thing is.

clue.text: Expression of annoyance from bishop when in late regularly

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: one word placed in the other, sitting between its letters
at regular intervals, so every other letter of the word is kept

parts.note: first and third letters
as and when both mean at the time that

explanation.surface: A bishop curses at someone who keeps turning up late.
explanation.definitionFit: Blast is a mild exclamation of irritation, like damn or drat.

clue.text: German poet wearing excellent new English coat

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for German

indicators.note: someone wearing something has it around them, so the poet goes inside

parts.note: A1 means excellent, with the 1 read as the letter I
a bard is a poet
N is the abbreviation for new
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A German poet sports a fine new English overcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is an old rating for first-class quality, and the digit 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabardine is a tightly woven twill fabric, and also the name of a raincoat made from it.

clue.text: Treat as insignificant piece of felt tile bent back

indicators.note: going back means the run of letters is read from right to left
a piece of something is only part of it, so the letters sit within the following words

parts.note: a run of letters spanning these three words

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a buckled piece of felt roofing tile as unimportant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the hidden run; 'back' does the turning.
explanation.definitionFit: To belittle someone is to make them or their achievements seem small and unimportant.

clue.text: Swinging handbag, daughter knocks out penultimate member of gang in foreign capital

indicators.note: something swinging moves about, so the letters are shaken into a new order
what is knocked out is removed from the word

parts.note: anagram fodder
the next-to-last letter, to be removed
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A daughter swinging her handbag fells a gang member in a foreign city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penultimate member of gang' sounds like a person but means the next-to-last letter of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Baghdad is the capital city of Iraq, so for a British setter a capital abroad.

clue.text: Aircraft manoeuvres in wind, climbing …

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means going upwards, so the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: to wind thread is to spool it

explanation.surface: A plane twists and turns in the wind as it gains height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' reads as moving air; here it is the verb meaning to coil.
explanation.definitionFit: Loops are aerobatic manoeuvres in which a plane flies a full vertical circle.

clue.text: … doubly a trial for one on maiden flight?

parts.note: first sense: an examination or try-out
a second word for a trial, as in a pilot scheme

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, a plane on its first flight is being put through its paces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubly' asks for two words that each mean a trial, side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A test pilot flies new aircraft to check them, so is aboard a maiden flight; the question mark flags this example.

clue.text: Republican shunned by monarchy left instead to committed following

indicators.note: shunned means pushed out, so that letter leaves the word
instead means taking the place of what was removed

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
the royal family as an institution
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A republican rejected by the crown has defected to a devoted band of supporters.
explanation.definitionFit: Loyalty is faithful devotion, the steadfast support a committed following shows.

clue.text: Clearly my usual bingo suffered following university

indicators.note: coming after, so the reworked letters are placed behind the single letter

parts.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university

indicators.note: something that has suffered is damaged and knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A student laments that their regular bingo night has plainly gone badly.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something unambiguously means saying it clearly, leaving no room for doubt or misunderstanding.

clue.text: Preserved sandwiches of last month it's learned

indicators.note: to sandwich something is to hold it between two layers, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: cured meat or fish is preserved by salting or smoking
ult., short for ultimo, means of last month in old business letters

explanation.surface: Leftover sandwiches from last month are being kept as an educational exhibit.
explanation.walkthrough: ULT (ultimo) is old commercial shorthand: 'your letter of the 5th ult.' meant last month.
explanation.definitionFit: A cultured person is well educated and refined, so learned is a fair synonym.

clue.text: Periodically slurp apple brandy finally in stock

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter of the phrase is kept

parts.note: first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, so its closing letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter

explanation.surface: Someone now and then drinks apple brandy from a well-stocked cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link: the wordplay ends up in, that is, means, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A supply is a stock or store of something kept available for use.

clue.text: Boxer consumes cabbage endlessly, it neutralises acid

indicators.note: what is consumed is taken inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the heavyweight champion

indicators.note: without its end, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: kale is a kind of cabbage

explanation.surface: A fighter eats greens as if they would settle his acid stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: An alkali is a base, a chemical substance which reacts with acids to neutralise them.

clue.text: Adjacent whisper admitting thirst

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: an aside is a remark said quietly
to thirst for is to long for

explanation.surface: A neighbour murmurs about being thirsty.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the whisper and the thirst work as verbs-turned-nouns here; 'thirst' gives the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Alongside means next to or beside, the same sense of position as adjacent.

clue.text: Verbally treat with contempt stage productions and shows

indicators.note: verbally means spoken out, so we go by the sound of the words

parts.note: to diss is slang for to disrespect
dramas put on in a theatre

explanation.surface: Someone speaks scornfully of theatre productions and exhibitions.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the slang word needs the sound: DISS said out loud gives the spelling DIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Displays and shows are both nouns for exhibitions put on for people to look at.

clue.text: Round his place oddly beginning to rage inside

indicators.note: inside means placed within the other letters
done oddly means done in a strange way, so the letters are put in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: the beginning of the word, so just its first letter is used

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Someone goes round his home strangely as anger starts to build.
explanation.definitionFit: Spherical means shaped like a ball, a solid form whose surface is round.

clue.text: Tree-dwelling snake's about, tip off Spanish royal

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards
with its tip removed, so the end letter is lost

parts.note: a cobra is a venomous hooded snake
real is Spanish for royal, as in Real Madrid

explanation.surface: A snake hanging about in the trees warns a Spanish king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip off' reads like a warning being given, but it trims the C off the turned word.
explanation.definitionFit: Arboreal animals such as monkeys and squirrels live in trees, so it describes tree-dwelling creatures.

clue.text: Raising fruit tree against wall, I overlooked return of disease

indicators.note: in a down entry raising means lifting upwards, so the word reads bottom to top
the letter I is overlooked, meaning missed out of the word

parts.note: an espalier is a fruit tree trained flat against a wall

explanation.surface: A gardener training a fruit tree on a wall misses a recurrence of blight.
explanation.walkthrough: An espalier is a tree grown flat on a frame or wall; drop its I and turn it upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A relapse is a patient's falling back into illness after an apparent recovery.

clue.text: Act inferior and unruly

parts.note: an Act of Parliament is a law
less means lower in rank or worth

explanation.surface: Someone behaving badly and being disorderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' looks like a verb, behave; it is the noun, a statute.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawless means not governed by or obeying laws, hence wild and unruly.

clue.text: It encourages rapid development in established case pursuing stolen barrels

indicators.note: chasing behind, so this part comes after the rest

parts.note: hot goods are stolen ones
b is the oil-industry abbreviation for barrels, as in b/d, barrels per day

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: Police chase stolen barrels in an established case.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotbed is a place or environment where something, often bad, grows and spreads quickly.

clue.text: Greek character crosses line with ill-treatment of ponies

indicators.note: one thing crossing into another goes within it
ill-treatment knocks things about, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: anagram fodder
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A Greek man oversteps the mark by mistreating ponies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' is a letter of an alphabet, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth letter of the Greek alphabet, a written character.

clue.text: Insult of little significance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a snub or affront, as a noun
second meaning: small or minor, as an adjective

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as describing a minor insult; in fact the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: One word serves as a noun for a snub and as an adjective meaning small or unimportant.

clue.text: Brown starts to take over after Blair's stint ends

indicators.note: the starts of the next words, so only their first letters are taken

parts.note: first letters

indicators.note: the ends of these words, so only their last letters are taken

parts.note: last characters of each word

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown begins to take over from Tony Blair once his period as prime minister ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown succeeded Tony Blair as UK prime minister in 2007; here 'Brown' is the verb, as with bread.
explanation.definitionFit: To toast bread is to brown it under heat.

clue.text: Possibly fluke throw that disfigures the grass

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the thing it describes, a noun

parts.note: a fluke is a parasitic flatworm, so it is possibly this
to cast is to throw

explanation.surface: A lucky throw seems to have ruined the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fluke' reads as a lucky chance; here it is the liver fluke, a parasitic flatworm.
explanation.definitionFit: A wormcast is the little coiled heap of soil an earthworm leaves on a lawn, spoiling its smooth surface.

clue.text: Thief's unpleasant to an Australian

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a criminal or swindler
second meaning: Australian slang for bad, nasty or unwell

explanation.surface: A thief is described as nasty by someone from Down Under.
explanation.definitionFit: Crook is a noun for a criminal and, in Australian English, an adjective meaning bad or ill.

clue.text: Top rival chose to work in Westminster perhaps

indicators.note: putting the words to work sets them in motion, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A leading competitor opted for a job in the seat of British government.
explanation.walkthrough: Westminster suggests Parliament, but here it is Westminster School, a famous fee-paying London school.
explanation.definitionFit: Westminster School is an example of a fee-paying independent school, so 'perhaps' flags an example.

clue.text: Soldiers needing time amongst some moving souvenirs

indicators.note: being amongst others means being placed in the middle of them
moving letters shift around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: needing means having alongside, so the soldiers come with the following letter

parts.note: soldiers are men in the ranks
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Troops find time for some emotional keepsakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' looks like it describes the souvenirs as touching, but it shuffles the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mementos are objects kept as reminders of a person or event, much like souvenirs.

clue.text: Fondness of musical, on no longer

indicators.note: the named little word is no longer there, so it is dropped from the title

parts.note: The Lion King, the Disney stage musical
the letters to be taken out

explanation.surface: A theatregoer's affection for a show that has closed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On no longer' sounds like a show that has finished its run; actually it removes ON from the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having a taste or affection for something, enjoying it, is the same warm feeling.
